The Transportation Problem
A special type of Linear Programming Problem.
Objective: To minimize transportation cost.
Used in logistics and supply chain.

What is a Transportation 
Problem?
A transportation problem deals with the distribution of a single 
homogeneous commodity from several sources (origins) to several 
destinations.
• There are multiple sources (origins) where goods are available. 
• There are multiple destinations where goods are required. 
• The cost of transportation from each source to each destination is 
known and may differ. 
• The objective is to minimize the total transportation cost while 
satisfying all supply constraints and meeting all demand 
requirements. 
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT

Consider the following situation:
• A fan manufacturing company has 𝑚 factories located in 𝑛 different cities. 
• The fans produced in these factories are supplied to 𝑛 retail dealers located in 𝑛 different cities.

Relation Between Assignment and Transportation Problem:
• An assignment problem is a simplified transportation problem,

Mathematically:

Important Terminologies
• Feasible solution: A feasible solution to a transportation problem is a set of non-negative individual allocations (≥ 0)
which satisfies the row and column sum restrictions.
• Basic feasible solution (BFS): A feasible solution of an 𝑚 by 𝑛 transportation problem is said to be basic if the total
number of positive allocations is equal to 𝑚 + 𝑛 − 1 (One less than the sum of the number of rows and columns).
• Optimum solution: A feasible solution (not necessarily basic) is said to be optimum if it minimizes the total
transportation cost.
• Non-degenerate Basic Feasible Solution: A BFS of a transportation problem is said to be non-degenerate BFS if the
allocations are in independent position.
(Independent positions of a set of allocations means that it is always impossible to form any closed loop through these
allocations.)
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT

Solution of a Transportation Problem
The solution of a transportation problem consists of the two steps:
• Step 1: To find an initial basic feasible solution.
• Step 2: To obtain an optimal solution by making successive improvements to initial basic 
feasible solution (obtained in step 1) until no further decrease in the transportation cost is 
possible.
Methods to find an Initial Basic Feasible Solution:
• Method 1: North-West Corner Rule.
• Method 2: Lowest Cost Entry (Matrix Minima) Method.
• Method 3: Unit Cost Penalty Method (Vogel's Approximation Method). 
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT

North-West 
Corner Rule.
Step 1:
• Start with the the top-most left corner, i.e., cell (1, 1). 
• Allocate there maximum possible amount. 
• Thus, 𝑥11 = min (𝑎1, 𝑏1).
Step 2: 
Case I: If 𝒃𝟏 < 𝒂𝟏: 𝑥11 = 𝑏1 and there is still some quantity 
available left in row 1. 
• Move to the right-hand cell, i.e., 1,2 .
• Make the second allocation amount 𝑥12 =
min(𝑎1 − 𝑥11, 𝑏2) in that cell.
Case II: If 𝒃𝟏 > 𝒂𝟏: 𝑥11 = 𝑎1 and there is still some requirement 
left in column 1. 
• Move vertically downwards to the next cel, i.e., (2,1).
• Make the second allocation amount 𝑥21 =
min(𝑎1, 𝑏1 − 𝑥11) in this cell.
Case III: If 𝒃𝟏 = 𝒂𝟏: 𝑥12 = 0 or 𝑥21 = 0.
• Start from the new north-west corner of the 
transportation table.
• Allocate their as much as possible.
Step 3: Repeat steps 1 and 2 until all the available quantity is exhausted or all 
the requirement is satisfied.
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT
• In this method we always move to the right or
down ⟹ No loop can be formulated by
drawing horizontal and vertical lines to the
allocations.
• At each allocation at least one row or column
is discarded from further consideration.
• The last allocation discards both a row and a
column simultaneously.
• We cannot get more than (m + 𝑛 −
1) individual positive allocations ⟹ We
always get non-degenerate basic feasible
solution.

Unit Cost 
Penalty Method 
(Vogel's 
Approximation 
Method).
Step 1: 
• Identify the smallest and second smallest costs for each row of the transportation table.
• Find the difference between them for each row. 
• Write these differences alongside the transportation table against the respective rows by 
enclosing them in parentheses. These are called 'penalties’.
• Write the similar differences for each column below the corresponding column. 
Step 2: 
• Select the row or column for which the penalty is the largest.
• If a tie occurs, use any arbitrary tie breaking choice. 
• Allocate the maximum possible amount to the cell with lowest cost in that particular 
row or column. 
• Let the largest penalty correspond to 𝑖
th row and let 𝑐𝑖𝑗 be the smallest cost in the 𝑖
th
row. Allocate the amount 𝑥ij = min (𝑎i
, 𝑏j) in the cell (𝑖,𝑗). 
• Cross out the 𝑖
th row or the 𝑗
th column in the usual manner and construct the reduced 
matrix.
Step 3: 
• Compute the row and column penalties for the reduced transportation table.
• Repeat the step 2. 
• Continue this process until all the available quantity is exhausted or all the requirement 
is satisfied. Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT
NOTE: If in the selected row or column the minimum cost is not unique, then locate in that cell 
in which more allocations can be made.

Loops and 
their 
Properties
Loop: An ordered set of four or more cells in a
transportation table is said to form a loop if
a) Any two adjacent cells of the set lie
either in the same row or in the same
column.
b) No three or more adjacent cells lie in the
same row or in the same column.
NOTE:
• The first cell of the set follows the last one in the set.
• If we join the cells of a loop by horizontal and
vertical line segments we get a closed path.
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT
Properties:
1. Every loop has an even number of cells.
2. A feasible solution to a transportation problem is basic iff, the corresponding cells in
the transportation table do not form a loop.

Optimality Test
• After obtaining an initial
BFS to a given transportation
problem, we need to test it
for optimality, i.e., whether
or not the solution minimizes
the total transportation cost.
• Optimality test is applicable
to a non-degenerate BFS,
i.e., to a feasible solution
consisting of ( 𝑚 + 𝑛 − 1 )
allocations in independent
positions.
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT
Computational Procedure of Optimality Test
Step1: Determine a set of (𝑚 + 𝑛) numbers 𝑢𝑖 (𝑖 = 1,2, … , 𝑚) and 𝑣𝑗 (𝑗 =
1,2, … , 𝑛 ) such that for each occupied cell (𝑟, 𝑠)
c𝑟𝑠 = 𝑢𝑟 + 𝑣𝑠
.
Step2: Compute the cell evaluation 𝑑𝑖𝑗 for each unoccupied cell (𝑖,𝑗) using the 
formula 
𝑑𝑖𝑗 = c𝑖𝑗 − 𝑢𝑖 + 𝑣𝑗
.
Step3: Examine the matrix of cell evaluations as follows:
a) If all 𝑑𝑖𝑗 > 0, then the solution under test is optimal and unique.
b) If all 𝑑𝑖𝑗 ≥ 0, with at least one 𝑑𝑖𝑗 = 0 , then the solution under test 
is optimal and alternative optimal solution exists.
c) If at least one 𝑑𝑖𝑗 < 0, then the solution under test is not optimal.

Transportation Algorithm for Minimization Problem 
(MODI Method)
Step V: (When at least one 𝑑𝑖𝑗 < 0)
• Select the min (most negative) 𝑑𝑖𝑗.
• Form a closed loop by joining this cell of min 𝑑𝑖𝑗
with the cells of positive allocations.
• Allocate to this cell as much as possible by vacating
at least one of the pre-occupied cells and
maintaining the row and column sum restrictions.
• This will give a new (improved) BFS.
Step VI:
• Repeat the Steps III to V to test the optimality of this
new BFS.
• Continue the process until an optimum basic
feasible solution is obtained.

Step I:
• Construct transportation table entering the capacities

• Otherwise, go to Step V.

Degeneracy in Transportation Problems
• A BFS to an m-origin and n-destination transportation problem
can have at-most ( 𝑚 + 𝑛 − 1 ) independent non-zero
allocations.
• If the number of allocation is exactly (𝑚 + 𝑛 − 1), the BFS is
said to be non-degenerate otherwise it is said to be a degenerate
one.
• Degeneracy in transportation problem can occur in two ways :
(i) BFS may be degenerate from the initial stage
onward.
(ii) It may become degenerate at any intermediate stage,
when the selection one entering cell empties two or
more pre-occupied cells simultaneously.
• To resolve degeneracy, we allocate an extremely small amount
Δ (close to zero) to one or more unoccupied cells of the matrix
(generally lowest cost cells if possible), so that the total
number of occupied cells become (𝑚 + 𝑛 − 1) at independent
positions.
Dr. Soniya Dhama, RGIPT
• Δ satisfies the following conditions:
1) Δ < 𝑥ij for 𝑥ij > 0.
2) 𝑥ij + Δ = 𝑥ij = 𝑥ij − Δ for 𝑥ij > 0.
3) Δ + 0 = Δ.
4) If there are more than one Δ introduced in the 
solution :
• If Δ, Δ' are in the same row :
𝜟 < 𝜟' when 𝜟 is to the left to 𝜟'.
• If Δ, Δ' are in the same column: 
𝜟 < 𝜟' when 𝜟 is above 𝜟'.
• Even after introducing Δ, the original solution of the 
problem is not changed. 
• It is only a technique to apply the optimality test. 
• As Δ has no physical significance, ultimately it is to be 
omitted.
